Conceptual Physics — Unit 1 Canonical Bank

Forces, Motion, and Equilibrium

Unit mastery goals

  • U1-MG01: Use evidence and models to distinguish observations, inferences, and testable physics explanations, and communicate what a representation or relationship means.
  • U1-MG02: Explain Newton's First Law and inertia to predict when an object's motion remains unchanged or changes.
  • U1-MG03: Represent and determine net force using vectors, then use the result to classify balanced and unbalanced situations.
  • U1-MG04: Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

1.1 Thinking Like a Physicist

Learning target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

  • I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.
  • I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.
  • I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

Whats To Come

U1-S1-WTC01

Whats To Come · DOK 2 · instructional
A student watches a toy car roll across a table and records: (1) the car moved 82 cm in 4.0 s; (2) the car seemed to slow near the edge; (3) the table must be slightly rough; (4) a motion model can summarize what changed. Sort statements 1-3 as direct observation/measurement or inference, then write one testable question that could distinguish between two explanations for the slowing.
Teacher answer / solution
Statement 1 is a measurement/observation. Statement 2 is an observation if based directly on the motion seen or measured. Statement 3 is an inference. A valid testable question could compare motion on surfaces with different roughness while holding the car and release method constant.
Learning target
Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

Notes Example

U1-S1-NOTE-EX01

Notes Example · DOK 2 · instructional
A motion sensor reports positions of 0.20 m, 0.44 m, and 0.68 m at successive times. A student writes, "The cart is trying to move away from the sensor." Identify the observation/measurement and the inference.
Teacher answer / solution
The reported positions are measurements. The claim about what the cart is "trying" to do is an inference because intention was not directly measured.

U1-S1-NOTE-EX02

Notes Example · DOK 2 · instructional
A claim says, "Objects fall faster on Tuesdays." Explain why the wording can be scientific only if a test can produce evidence that might support or contradict it. Propose one controlled comparison.
Teacher answer / solution
A scientific claim must be testable and open to being contradicted by evidence. One could drop the same object from the same height under comparable conditions on Tuesdays and other days and compare measured fall times.

U1-S1-NOTE-EX03

Notes Example · DOK 2 · instructional
The relationship $d=vt$ is used for constant-speed motion. Explain what each symbol represents and what the relationship communicates physically before calculating anything.
Teacher answer / solution
Distance traveled d is related to speed v and elapsed time t. At constant speed, distance increases in direct proportion to time; doubling the time doubles the distance for the same speed.

U1-S1-NOTE-EX04

Notes Example · DOK 2 · instructional
Two explanations fit the same first observation. Explanation A predicts the cart should travel farther on a smoother surface. Explanation B predicts surface type should not matter. Describe evidence that could distinguish the explanations and why one successful trial is not enough for a strong conclusion.
Teacher answer / solution
Compare repeated trials on surfaces that differ in roughness while controlling the cart and release. Consistent distance or speed-change differences can distinguish the predictions. Repeats reduce the chance that a single unusual result controls the conclusion.

Notes You Try It

U1-S1-NOTE-YTI01

Notes You Try It · DOK 2 · instructional
A thermometer reads 21.4 C, then 23.1 C after a lamp is turned on. A student says, "The lamp is heating the air." Separate the measurement from the inference and state what additional evidence would strengthen the claim.
Teacher answer / solution
The temperatures are measurements; attributing the change to the lamp is an inference/explanation. Repeated trials with a comparison condition, such as no lamp, would strengthen the claim.

U1-S1-NOTE-YTI03

Notes You Try It · DOK 2 · instructional
A model says $W=mg$. Without calculating, explain what the model says about weight when mass increases while the local gravitational field stays the same.
Teacher answer / solution
Weight is proportional to mass when g is unchanged. More mass corresponds to greater weight; doubling mass doubles weight.

Two models predict different outcomes when a hanging mass is doubled. Model A predicts twice the measured effect; Model B predicts no change. State a measurement plan that could compare the models.

Measure the outcome for the original hanging mass and for double the mass while holding other relevant conditions fixed, repeat trials, then compare the measured change with both model predictions.

Exit Ticket A

U1-S1-ET-A-Q01

Exit Ticket A · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
A student writes: "The cart traveled 62 cm; therefore the wheels are worn." Identify the observation and inference and state one testable follow-up.
Teacher answer / solution
The direct observation is that the cart traveled 62 cm. The claim that the wheels are worn is an inference. A testable follow-up could compare repeated travel measurements using the same cart and release before and after changing or inspecting the wheels while controlling the surface.
Learning target
Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

Two explanations predict different cart travel distances on rough and smooth surfaces. Describe the evidence needed to decide which explanation is better supported.

Exit Ticket C

U1-S1-ET-C-Q01

Exit Ticket C · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
Explain what $d=vt$ communicates physically for constant speed and give one reason treating it only as a calculation recipe can lead to weak reasoning.
Teacher answer / solution
In $d=vt$ for constant speed d is distance v is constant speed and t is elapsed time. The relationship communicates that distance grows in direct proportion to time at fixed speed. Treating it only as a substitution recipe can hide assumptions and prevent qualitative prediction or interpretation.
Learning target
Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

1.2 Forces and Newton's First Law

Learning target: Students will explain Newton's First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object's motion will stay the same or change.

  • I can state Newton's First Law in everyday language.
  • I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.
  • I can distinguish between no forces acting and no net force acting and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

Whats To Come

U1-S2-WTC01

Whats To Come · DOK 2 · instructional
Imagine a puck gliding on an almost frictionless surface. After the brief push ends, which information would you need to decide whether its motion should remain unchanged: its current speed, its mass, the net force acting after the push, or the distance already traveled? Rank the information from most physically decisive to least and explain your ranking.
Teacher answer / solution
The net force after the push is decisive for whether velocity changes. Current speed describes the motion but does not by itself determine whether it will change. Mass affects inertia but zero net force still means unchanged velocity. Distance already traveled does not determine the future motion.
Learning target
Students will explain Newton's First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object's motion will stay the same or change.

Notes Example

U1-S2-NOTE-EX01

Notes Example · DOK 2 · instructional
State Newton's First Law in everyday language, then apply it to a hockey puck gliding at constant velocity after the stick is no longer touching it.
Teacher answer / solution
If the net external force is zero, an object keeps its state of motion: rest stays rest and constant straight-line motion continues. The puck does not need a continuing forward net force to keep moving; if forces balance, its velocity remains unchanged.
Learning target
Students will explain Newton's First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object's motion will stay the same or change.

Exit Ticket A · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
A cart moves straight at constant velocity after a push ends. Explain the motion using Newton's First Law and inertia without describing inertia as a force.
Teacher answer / solution
After the push ends the cart can continue at constant velocity if the external forces sum to zero. Newton's First Law says zero net force means velocity remains unchanged. Inertia is the cart's mass-related resistance to velocity change; it is not a forward force.
Learning target
Students will explain Newton's First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object's motion will stay the same or change.
I can
I can state Newton's First Law in everyday language.
Mastery goal

Exit Ticket B

U1-S2-ET-B-Q01

Exit Ticket B · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
A book rests on a table. Draw or describe the forces on the book and explain how "forces act" can be true at the same time as "net force is zero."
Teacher answer / solution
Earth pulls downward on the book with weight and the table pushes upward with support force. For a resting book those forces can be equal and opposite so their vector sum is zero. Individual forces therefore act even though the net force is zero.
Learning target
Students will explain Newton's First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object's motion will stay the same or change.

Exit Ticket C

U1-S2-ET-C-Q01

Exit Ticket C · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
Correct the claim: "A forward force is needed to keep an object moving." Use a specific motion example in your correction.
Teacher answer / solution
A forward net force is not required to maintain motion. For example a puck moving in a straight line at constant velocity can have zero net force. A nonzero net force is needed to change velocity not simply to have velocity.
Learning target
Students will explain Newton's First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object's motion will stay the same or change.

1.3 Net Force and Vectors

Learning target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

  • I can explain why force is a vector quantity.
  • I can combine forces acting in the same direction or opposite directions.
  • I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.

Whats To Come

U1-S3-WTC01

Whats To Come · DOK 2 · instructional
Two horizontal force arrows act on the cart. Without doing more than one subtraction, predict the direction of the resultant and describe how the arrow for the resultant should compare with the two shown arrows.
Teacher answer / solution
The resultant points right because the rightward force is larger. Its magnitude is 2 N, so the resultant arrow should point right and be shorter than either original force arrow.
Learning target
Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.
I can

Exit Ticket C

U1-S3-ET-C-Q01

Exit Ticket C · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
A force model has 7 N right, 7 N left, 5 N up, and 3 N down. Determine the net-force vector and predict the direction of velocity change.
Teacher answer / solution
The 7 N right and 7 N left forces cancel. Vertically 5 N up - 3 N down = 2 N up. The net-force vector is 2 N up so the velocity changes in an upward sense.

1.4 Equilibrium and Balanced Motion

Learning target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

  • I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
  • I can explain why an object at rest can still have forces acting on it.
  • I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.

Whats To Come

U1-S4-WTC01

Whats To Come · DOK 2 · instructional
Two identical carts are observed for 6 s. Cart A remains at rest. Cart B moves east at a constant 2 m/s in a straight line. For each cart, decide whether equilibrium is possible. Then identify one kind of evidence that would be needed before claiming the forces are balanced.
Teacher answer / solution
Both carts can be in mechanical equilibrium because zero net force is consistent with rest or constant straight-line velocity. Evidence could include a valid force diagram, force measurements showing opposing forces balance, or motion data showing no change in velocity.
Learning target
Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.
I can
I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
Mastery goal

Notes Example

U1-S4-NOTE-EX01

Notes Example · DOK 2 · instructional
A backpack rests on a floor. Explain why this can be static equilibrium even though gravity acts on it.
Teacher answer / solution
Static equilibrium means the net force is zero while the object is at rest. The downward weight can be balanced by an upward support force from the floor.

Exit Ticket A

U1-S4-ET-A-Q01

Exit Ticket A · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
A cart moves east at constant velocity while a 28 N pull acts east. Determine the opposing horizontal force and explain why the cart can be in dynamic equilibrium.
Teacher answer / solution
Constant straight-line velocity means zero net force. The 28 N east pull therefore requires a 28 N west opposing horizontal force. The cart is in dynamic equilibrium because it is moving while its net force is zero.
Learning target
Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

Exit Ticket B

U1-S4-ET-B-Q01

Exit Ticket B · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
A student says a car traveling around a curve at constant speed is in equilibrium. Evaluate the claim using velocity and net force.
Teacher answer / solution
The claim is incorrect. Constant speed does not mean constant velocity when direction changes. A car following a curve has changing velocity and therefore nonzero acceleration and a nonzero net force directed toward the inside of the turn.

Exit Ticket C

U1-S4-ET-C-Q01

Exit Ticket C · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
A hanging sign weighs 95 N and is motionless. Determine the upward support and explain why forces do not disappear at equilibrium.
Teacher answer / solution
Because the sign is motionless its vertical net force is zero. The upward support must therefore be 95 N to balance the 95 N weight. The individual forces remain present even though they cancel.
Learning target
Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.
I can
I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
Mastery goal
U1-MG03
Practice
systems reasoning; model-based explanation; argument from evidence

1.5 Modeling Forces in the Real World

Learning target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

  • I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.
  • I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.
  • I can explain how the net force affects the object's motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Whats To Come

U1-S5-WTC01

Whats To Come · DOK 2 · instructional
A delivery box slides right across a warehouse floor while a worker pushes it. Three classmates draw different force models: one includes only the push, one includes push and weight, and one includes push, friction, support, and weight. Before deciding which model is best, write the rule you would use to decide which forces belong on a force diagram for the box.
Teacher answer / solution
Include forces exerted on the chosen object by other objects/interactions. For the box, a complete simple model can include the worker push, floor friction, floor support, and Earth's gravitational force (weight). Do not include forces the box exerts on other objects.
Learning target
Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.
I can
I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.
Mastery goal

Practice
develop/evaluate models; scientific explanation; argument from evidence

U1-S5-NOTE-EX02

Notes Example · DOK 2 · instructional
A student draws a force diagram for a sled being pulled right and includes "sled pulls person left" as an arrow on the sled. Critique the diagram.
Teacher answer / solution
That arrow describes a force exerted by the sled on the person, not a force acting on the sled. A sled diagram should include forces acting on the sled, such as the person/rope pull, friction if relevant, support, and weight.

U1-S5-NOTE-EX03

Notes Example · DOK 2 · instructional
A box moves right while the force model shows 10 N right and 10 N left horizontally, with vertical forces balanced. Predict the immediate motion behavior from the model and explain what the diagram cannot tell you by itself.
Teacher answer / solution
The model gives zero net force, so the velocity should remain unchanged: rest would remain rest or existing constant straight-line motion would continue. The diagram alone does not specify the current velocity unless motion information is also provided.

Exit Ticket A

U1-S5-ET-A-Q01

Exit Ticket A · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
A model for a box moving on a rough floor includes push, support, weight, and a forward motion force but omits friction. Critique and revise the model.
Teacher answer / solution
Remove the forward motion-force arrow because motion is not an interaction force. Include friction opposite the sliding direction if the floor is rough along with the applied push support force and weight. Only actual external interactions acting on the box belong on its force model.
Learning target
Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exit Ticket B

U1-S5-ET-B-Q01

Exit Ticket B · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
A force model predicts a 4 N right net force, but motion data show constant straight-line velocity. Explain the conflict and what should be checked or revised.
Teacher answer / solution
A 4 N right net force predicts a rightward change in velocity. Constant straight-line velocity instead requires zero net force so the model and evidence conflict. Recheck measured motion and the force inventory or magnitudes then revise the model so the resultant matches reliable evidence.
Learning target
Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exit Ticket C

U1-S5-ET-C-Q01

Exit Ticket C · DOK 2-3 · formative-secure
Choose a sled as the system. Describe a complete force model for a sled accelerating right across rough snow and explain how the model supports the motion prediction.
Teacher answer / solution
For the sled system include weight downward support from the snow upward a rightward pull and leftward friction or drag. Because the sled accelerates right the rightward pull must exceed the leftward resistance while the vertical forces may balance. The resulting net force points right consistent with the observed velocity change.
Learning target
Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Performance Task

U1-PERF01

Performance Task · DOK 3-4 · secure
Cart Surface Model Defense
A class tests the same cart on two level surfaces using the same starting speed. Average observations are shown below.
SurfaceStart speedSpeed after 3 sDistance in 3 s
A1.2 m/s1.1 m/s3.45 m
B1.2 m/s0.5 m/s2.45 m
(a) State a claim about the relative horizontal net force on the cart on the two surfaces. (b) Draw or describe a qualitative force model for each surface after release. (c) Cite two pieces of data as evidence. (d) Explain why the evidence supports the models using Newton's First Law. (e) Identify one additional control or repeated measurement that would strengthen the investigation.
Teacher answer / solution
(a) Surface B has the larger resistive horizontal net force because its velocity decreases much more in the same time. Surface A is closer to zero horizontal net force. (b) Both models include balanced support and weight. After release there is no continuing hand force. Surface A has a small leftward resistance; Surface B has a larger leftward resistance. (c) Both start at 1.2 m/s, but after 3 s A is 1.1 m/s while B is 0.5 m/s; A also travels farther, 3.45 m versus 2.45 m. (d) Newton's First Law says velocity remains unchanged only when net force is zero. The greater decrease on B is evidence of a larger nonzero net force opposite the motion. (e) Valid improvements include repeated trials, same cart/wheels, same release method, same surface level, and calibrated motion measurement.
Scoring: Credit accurate model selection/revision, correct net-force reasoning, explicit evidence-to-claim links, and physically correct interpretation. Requirements: 15-25 min; calculator optional; no lab materials required for the paper version

U1-PERF02

Performance Task · DOK 3-4 · secure
Force-Model Repair Challenge
A student submits this description for a box sliding right at constant velocity across a rough floor: "Weight is 40 N down. Support is 40 N up. A 12 N push acts right. Friction is 5 N left. A 7 N motion force acts left to make the forces balance. Inertia pushes right to keep the box moving." (a) Identify every incorrect or unnecessary force claim. (b) Revise the horizontal force model so it is consistent with constant velocity. (c) Calculate the required friction force if the applied push is 12 N right. (d) Explain why the corrected model is consistent with Newton's First Law. (e) Write one sentence that clearly distinguishes inertia from force.
Teacher answer / solution
(a) Motion force and inertia force are not valid interaction forces. The stated 5 N friction cannot coexist with only a 12 N right push and constant velocity unless another real 7 N left interaction is identified. (b) A simple corrected model has 12 N push right and 12 N friction left; 40 N support up and 40 N weight down. (c) Friction must be 12 N left. (d) All components then sum to zero, so constant straight-line velocity is consistent with Newton's First Law. (e) Inertia is the mass-related property that resists changes in velocity; it is not an additional force arrow.
Scoring: Credit accurate model selection/revision, correct net-force reasoning, explicit evidence-to-claim links, and physically correct interpretation. Requirements: 15-20 min; no calculator required
Learning target

Mastery goal

  3. Only stationary objects can have zero net force.
  4. Inertia is the balancing force.
Teacher answer / solution
Moving at constant velocity in a straight line is compatible with zero net force.
Correct choice: B

U1-SUM-V6-Q08

Summative · DOK 3 · secure
A student writes, 'The cart keeps moving because the push remains stored inside it.' Rewrite the explanation using Newton's First Law.
Teacher answer / solution
Once contact ends the push force ends. If the remaining external forces sum to zero, the cart continues with constant velocity; no stored force is required.

U1-SUM-V6-Q09

Summative · DOK 3 · secure
Compare Case A: a book at rest with balanced support/weight; Case B: a puck moving straight at constant velocity with balanced forces. Explain the shared force rule and the different motion states.
Teacher answer / solution
Both have zero net force, so velocity is unchanged. In Case A the unchanged velocity is zero; in Case B it is a nonzero constant straight-line velocity.

U1-SUM-V6-Q10

Summative · DOK 3 · secure
Choose a combined cart-plus-rider as the system. Explain why the forces the cart and rider exert on each other are not external forces on the combined system, and name two external forces that may still act.
Teacher answer / solution
Cart-rider interactions are internal because both objects are inside the system boundary. External forces can include Earth's weight, track support, friction/drag, or an outside push/pull.
